title: The Hardworking Lifter who BROKE the Natty Limit (Alex Leonidas)
summary: Lifter-profile episode on natural lifter Alex Leonidas. NH goes through Alex's low-frequency upper/lower plus push/pull split, built on two hard sets per exercise and paired 'twin' exercises, then his training philosophy (a calisthenics base, Westside influence, bulks and cuts tied to goals) and grades each muscle group. He uses Alex as proof that the natural limit doesn't exist and that minimalism fails for arms.
claims: Alex Leonidas is credited with starting the rebirth of natural lifting content on YouTube
Most of Alex's mass came from years of full body 2x/week inspired by Westside Barbell, which is the strength method closest to bodybuilding
Alex trains mostly 6-8 reps, max about 10, with high intensity, medium volume and low frequency
Open the session with the variation that targets your weak area (Alex: incline press for upper chest) since that is when you are freshest
NH applies the same idea by opening with hammer or pinwheel curls because his brachioradialis lags his biceps
Two high-stability movements like incline dumbbell press and wide pull-ups are best not superset, because both demand full focus
Super-wide pull-ups are tremendous for lats and V-taper
The barrel press is a biomechanically sound fly alternative: more stretch, less shoulder and elbow stress, more load
Doing 2 hard sets each of two similar exercises avoids the intensity loss of 4 straight sets in low-frequency training
Deficit handstand push-ups are the best calisthenics shoulder movement
Upper back is a volume black hole: as long as the lower back isn't taxed, it recovers from lots of work
Opening with an isolation exercise for a weak point is pointless; isolation suffers less from fatigue and fits after compounds
Light hammer curl + pushdown superset can warm up cranky elbows before extensions
Minimalism works for big compound-trained muscles but not for arms; Alex's arms grew once he dropped it
A 4-set arm superset takes about 20 minutes once a week
Upper days should be about twice as long as lower days because each lower lift hits several muscles
Alex trains legs once a week and still has great legs, showing low leg frequency works
Heavy deadlift singles aren't optimal for hypertrophy; keep low-stimulus, high-fatigue work to a minimum, e.g. one rep at RPE 9
The SSB squat may be the best quad variation; Alex does it 3x10 at 2 RIR
Two heavy hip hinges in one session (deadlift plus good morning) is counterproductive for most people
After heavy compounds, move to lower-fatigue isolation like weighted sissy squats and Nordics; that last 20% makes the physique
Supersets don't cost performance; Alex supersets incline press with chest-supported rows
Three set schemes: hard sets plus back-off sets (strength), 3-4 straight sets (NH), or 2 sets each of twin exercises (explosive lifters)
Cutting range of motion on a third press (dip machine) or doing strict t-bar rows can be smart in context
Whether a lift is good depends on what you want from it in that program
NH trains high frequency because he cannot produce Alex's per-session intensity; stronger lifters need longer recovery windows
Calisthenics gives perhaps the best base for later bodybuilding
A bodybuilder takes what works for hypertrophy from every sport
Low frequency needs high volume and intensity; high frequency can't sustain high volume
Bulks and cuts make sense when tied to a performance goal (a lift, a show, one-arm pull-ups)
Alex reached big chin-up numbers but his biceps stayed mediocre; no single lift does everything
Natural lifters are self-aware about weak points; mediocre enhanced lifters keep the same weak points for years
Alex keeps improving every year, showing the natural limit does not exist
Alex built both a big chest and shoulders by specializing separately in horizontal and vertical presses
The neck shrinks quickly if you stop isolating it because compounds don't train it
Poor leverages for pulls let glutes and lower back take over, leaving hamstrings to be isolated with knee flexion
Calisthenics athletes' abs look good only when lean; gaining weight reveals undeveloped abs
Grades for Alex: chest S, shoulders S+, lateral triceps A, long head B, biceps B (from C), forearms S, neck B, traps S, lats S, teres A, erectors A, abs B, quads A, hamstrings B, calves C
